title: If Only…
goals: Express wishes about the present with wish / if only + past (I wish I had more time; I wish you would listen).

learn.title: wish / if only + past: wishes about the present
learn.html:
We use wish (or if only, which is more emphatic) to express that we would like reality to be different. The verb goes one tense "further back": the opposite is true now.

StructureExampleReality
wish + simple pastI wish I had more free time.I don't have free time.
wish + were (all persons)I wish I were less busy. / If only he were here.I'm very busy. / He isn't here.
wish + couldWe wish we could afford a bigger flat.We can't afford it.
wish + subject + wouldI wish you would listen. / I wish it would stop raining.Someone else's behavior bothers me; I want it to change.
  • Were is the correct form in formal writing; in speech you often hear I wish I was.
  • wish + would is not used with I or with situations that nobody controls voluntarily: not I wish I would be taller (correct: I wish I were taller).
  • If only sounds more emotional: If only I knew the answer!

watch.wrong: I wish I have more time.
watch.right: I wish I had more time.
watch.why: Wish + simple past, even when we are talking about the present.

watch.wrong: I wish I would be taller.
watch.why: With I and a state: wish + were, not would.

watch.wrong: I wish you stopped making noise.
watch.right: I wish you would stop making noise.
watch.why: To complain about someone's behavior: wish + would.

learn.title: wish / if only + past perfect: regrets
learn.html:
To regret something that happened (or didn't happen) we use wish / if only + past perfect (had + past participle). Regret is also expressed with regret + -ing.

StructureExampleWhat actually happened
wish + had + past participleI wish I had studied harder.I didn't study enough.
wish + hadn't + past participleIf only we hadn't argued last night.We argued.
wish + could have + past participleI wish I could have gone to the concert.I couldn't go.
regret + -ingI regret not taking a gap year. / I regret telling him.Regret about something done or not done.

Wish + would have does not exist in this use: you don't say I wish I would have told her (correct: I wish I had told her). Common contractions: I'd studied (= I had studied), we hadn't left.

watch.wrong: I wish I studied harder at school.
watch.right: I wish I had studied harder at school.
watch.why: A regret about the past requires had + past participle.

watch.wrong: I wish I would have told her the truth.
watch.right: I wish I had told her the truth.
watch.why: After wish, would have is not used; use had + past participle.

watch.wrong: If only I didn't say that.
watch.right: If only I hadn't said that.

watch.wrong: I wish I had went to the party.
watch.right: I wish I had gone to the party.
watch.why: Had + past participle (gone), not simple past (went).

learn.title: Third conditional: if + had + past participle, would have + past participle
learn.html:
We imagine how the past would have been if something had been different. You already know the second conditional (If I had time, I would go); the third goes one tense further back.

FormStructureExample
AffirmativeIf + had + past participle, would have + past participleIf I had known, I would have called you.
NegativeIf + hadn't + past participle, wouldn't have + past participleIf she hadn't missed the bus, she wouldn't have been late.
Possibilitymight have / could haveIf we had left earlier, we could have caught the train.
QuestionWhat would you have done if…?What would you have done if you had lost your passport?
ContractedIf I'd known, I'd have called.'d = had (in the if clause) and would (in the result).

The if clause can come before or after the main clause; if it comes first, use a comma. The if clause never takes would have.

watch.wrong: If I would have studied, I would have passed.
watch.right: If I had studied, I would have passed.
watch.why: The if clause takes had + past participle, not would have.

watch.wrong: If he had left earlier, he wouldn't miss the flight.
watch.right: If he had left earlier, he wouldn't have missed the flight.
watch.why: The past result takes would have + past participle.

watch.wrong: If I had saw her, I would have said hello.
watch.right: If I had seen her, I would have said hello.

watch.wrong: What would you do if you had been me?
watch.right: What would you have done if you had been me?
watch.why: Imaginary past situation: would have done.

learn.title: Mixed conditionals: past and present combined
learn.html:
Sometimes an imaginary past has consequences now, or a current characteristic explains something that didn't happen.

TypeStructureExample
Past → present resultIf + had + past participle, would + base verbIf I had taken that job, I would be living in Toronto now.
Current situation → past resultIf + simple past (were), would have + past participleIf I weren't so shy, I would have asked her out.
  • Clues: now, today, still, these days appear in the present result.
  • The result can take could or might: If I had studied medicine, I might be a doctor now.

watch.wrong: If I had studied medicine, I would have been a doctor now.
watch.right: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
watch.why: Present result: would + base verb, not would have.

watch.wrong: If I was braver, I would ask her last year.
watch.right: If I were braver, I would have asked her last year.
watch.why: Past result: would have + past participle.

learn.title: Advice and criticism: should have, had better, if I were you
learn.html:
To give advice about the present or future, and to criticize or regret the past:

FunctionStructureExample
Advice (present)If I were you, I'd + base verbIf I were you, I'd take the scholarship.
Soft adviceYou might want to / Why don't you…?You might want to visit the campus first.
Strong warningYou'd better (not) + base verbYou'd better call him before it's too late.
Criticism / regretshould have / shouldn't have + past participleYou should have told me. I shouldn't have said that.
Missed optioncould have + past participleYou could have asked for help.
Unnecessaryneedn't have + past participleYou needn't have bought flowers.

Had better and should are followed by the base verb without to. In If I were you we use were, and the advice takes I'd / I would.

watch.wrong: You had better to leave now.
watch.why: Had better + base verb without to.

watch.wrong: You should have told to me the truth.
watch.right: You should have told me the truth.

watch.wrong: I should went to the doctor earlier.
watch.right: I should have gone to the doctor earlier.

watch.wrong: If I were you, I will take it.
watch.right: If I were you, I'd take it.

learn.title: Advice, certainty and reactions
learn.html:
Adverbs of certainty with would

  • In affirmative sentences they go after would: I would definitely accept. I'd probably feel healthier.
  • In negative sentences they go before wouldn't: I definitely wouldn't tell him. I probably wouldn't go.

Giving advice and reacting

  • If I were you, I'd… — direct advice.
  • You might want to… / You could… — soft advice.
  • That would be awesome! / That'd be great. — reacting to a possibility.
  • What would you do if…? — I'd… / I wouldn't… — asking about imaginary situations.
  • Would you…? — Yes, I would. / No, I wouldn't. — short answer.
  • I should have… / If only I had… — regretting something in the past.

write.prompt: Write a text of 180 to 250 words about an important decision you made (or didn't make) and how your life might have been if you had decided otherwise. Include what you regret and what you wish were different today. Opening example: Five years ago I turned down a job offer in Monterrey. If I had accepted it, …
checklist: A complete third conditional (If I had …, I would have …)
Two wishes: one about the present (wish + past) and one about the past (wish + had + past participle)
2 expressions about decisions (take a risk, play it safe, sleep on it…)
An adverb of certainty with would (definitely, probably)
An if clause without would have; correct past participles
write.model:
Five years ago I turned down a job offer in Monterrey. If I had accepted it, I would have moved to a bigger city and my career would probably have taken off much faster. At the time, I was afraid to take a risk, so I played it safe and stayed in my hometown, where my family and friends were.

I slept on the decision for two weeks, and in the end I let fear choose for me. Honestly, I regret not taking that chance. If I had gone, I would definitely have met new people and learned a lot about myself. And if I had moved, I would be earning more money now, and I might be living in my own apartment instead of sharing one with my sister.

I sometimes wish I were braver. I also wish I had asked someone for advice, because I made the choice completely alone. If only I had talked to a mentor, I would have seen the opportunity more clearly.

Of course, there are good things about my decision too. I'm close to my parents, and I have a job I mostly enjoy. If I hadn't stayed, I wouldn't have met my partner. So I don't think my life is bad, but I still wonder what might have happened. The lesson I have learned is simple: next time, I will not let fear decide for me.

write.prompt: A friend writes to you: they have to choose between a stable job in their city and a risky opportunity in another country. Reply with an email of 180 to 250 words: ask hypothetical questions, give your advice and tell what you would do or what you already regret. Opening example: Hi Mateo, thanks for telling me about your dilemma. If I were you, …
targets: advice with If I were you
checklist: If I were you, I'd … at least once
A hypothetical question (What would you do if…?)
Should have / shouldn't have or could have for a past experience
You might want to / You'd better + base verb
An adverb of certainty placed correctly (I definitely wouldn't…)
A verb with a preposition (apologize for, depend on, congratulate on)
Friendly tone, opening and closing of the email
write.model:
Hi Mateo,

Thanks for telling me about your dilemma. If I were you, I'd think carefully about what matters most to you right now. What would you do if you knew the new job would not work out? And what would you regret more: staying or leaving?

Honestly, I think you should go, but only if you have some savings. You'd better check the cost of living in the new country before you decide, and you might want to talk to people who already live there. You could also ask the company if they will pay for your flight and the first month of accommodation.

I can tell you what I did wrong. Two years ago, I had a similar chance, and I should have accepted it, but I depended on my parents' opinion too much. I apologize for sounding so serious, but I definitely wouldn't make the same mistake again. I should have trusted myself. At the same time, I shouldn't have waited so long to decide, because the offer disappeared.

Whatever you choose, I congratulate you on being brave enough to think about it. Please keep me updated, and call me if you want to talk it through. I'm here for you.

Take care,
Andrés

reading.title: The Road Not Taken
reading.intro: Read the article about a difficult decision and answer.
paragraphs: Every month, thousands of people write to the advice column of a Mexican magazine with the same question: "Did I make the right choice?" This month, we publish the story of Laura Medina, a thirty-four-year-old engineer from Querétaro, who agreed that her experience might help other readers facing a difficult decision.

Ten years ago, Laura was offered a full scholarship to study robotics in Munich. It was a dream come true, but she hesitated. Her father was ill, her boyfriend didn't want to move abroad, and she had only a week to decide. "I made a list of pros and cons, and the cons won," she says. "I turned the scholarship down. I told myself that I could apply again the following year." She never did.

Laura's life since then has not been bad at all. She works at a good company, she got married, and she has a three-year-old daughter. Still, she sometimes thinks about the road not taken. "If I had gone to Munich, I would probably be leading a research team by now," she admits. "And if I hadn't been so afraid of disappointing everyone, I might have taken the risk. I wish I had trusted myself more." She is proud of her career and would never call her life a failure, but the question keeps coming back to her, usually late at night.

Surprisingly, Laura does not blame her family. Her father recovered, and he now says she shouldn't have given up her dream for him. "I would have been fine," he told her last year. "You should have gone." Her former boyfriend, who is now a close friend, feels guilty too. "He wishes he had been more supportive," she explains.

Psychologists say that people regret what they didn't do far more than what they did. "In the short term, we regret our mistakes," explains Dr. Ana Villaseñor, who has studied decision-making for twenty years. "But in the long term, we regret the chances we passed up." Her advice? "If you are in a similar situation, don't decide in a hurry, but don't wait forever either. Sleep on it, talk to people you trust, and ask yourself what you would regret more in ten years."

Laura took that advice to heart. Last month she enrolled in an online master's program in robotics. "It's not Munich," she says with a smile, "but I definitely wouldn't change the life I have. I just wish I had started sooner."

listening.title: Two job offers
listening.intro: Listen to the conversation between two friends. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Rubén, I need your advice. I got two job offers, and I can't make up my mind.
One is at a big bank here in Mexico City. The salary is great, but the hours are long. The other is at a small startup in Guadalajara. The pay is lower, though, and I'd have to move.
Hmm. If I were you, I'd think about what matters most. What would you do if money weren't an issue?
I'd definitely choose the startup. I'd probably learn much more there.
My mom lives here. If I moved, I wouldn't be able to see her every week. I wish she lived closer to Guadalajara.
I understand. But you could visit her on weekends. You might want to ask the startup about flexible hours too.
That's a good idea. I should have asked them about it in the interview.
It's not too late. You'd better call them before Friday, though.
You're right. If I hadn't talked to you, I would have just accepted the bank's offer.
Sleep on it, and call me tomorrow. And whatever you choose, you can count on me.
